headline: Star QB Launches Finance Series to Teach Gen Z Money Skills
meta_description: NFL quarterback Fernando Mendoza partners with US Bank to launch 'Finance with Fernando,' an educational video series helping Gen Z manage money responsibly.
summary_short: Heisman Trophy winner Fernando Mendoza is using his platform to teach Generation Z about financial responsibility through a new video series with US Bank.
body:
Fernando Mendoza, the NFL's #1 draft pick and holder of an MBA from Indiana University's Kelley School of Business, is trading playbook strategy for wallet wisdom. The 23-year-old Heisman Trophy winner has partnered with US Bank to launch Finance with Fernando, an educational video series designed to help Generation Z navigate money management in today's complex economy. "I'm Fernando Mendoza—star quarterback. But my true passion is fiscal responsibility," he said in a teaser for the upcoming series. "A practical guide for Gen Z to make the most of their money." While no episodes have been released yet, Mendoza has already demonstrated genuine insight into financial thinking. During a postgame press conference after Indiana's dominant 56–22 victory over Oregon in the Peach Bowl semifinal, he was asked about avoiding the trap of complacency after big wins. His answer—rooted in Stoic philosophy about delayed gratification—could serve as solid investment advice. "Delayed gratification is a concept that was brought up by Stoicism and by the Stoics. I think it's one of the greatest attributes."

This educational venture builds on Mendoza's established philanthropic track record. In recent years, he and his brother Alberto, a football star at Georgia Tech, raised $360,000 for multiple sclerosis research in honor of their mother, who lives with the disease. The effort culminated in a $500,000 donation to the National MS Society through the Mendoza Family Fund, accelerating progress toward a world free of MS. The quarterback's willingness to channel his platform toward financial education and health advocacy suggests he's thinking far beyond the field—toward a generation that needs accessible guidance on managing money responsibly.
